UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                     BEFORE THE
                       FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


                                                      )
Southwest Power Pool, Inc.                            )                  Docket No. ER26-1323-000
                                                      )


    COMMENTS OF THE SOLAR ENERGY INDUSTRIES ASSOCIATION IN SUPPORT


         The Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA)1 respectfully submits these comments in

support of Southwest Power Pool, Inc.’s (SPP) proposed revisions to its Open Access

Transmission Tariff (SPP Tariff) to establish a Conditional High Impact Large Load Service

(CHILLS)2 process that will allow High Impact Large Loads (HILLs)3 to be served with non-

firm conditional transmission service. Some of SEIA’s members are developing solar and

storage resources at scale throughout the SPP region to meet rising demand and support the

reliable integration of new, concentrated large loads. SPP’s CHILLS proposal is a necessary

complement to HILLs and will effectuate expedited large load integration. The Commission

should accept SPP’s filing as just, reasonable, and not unduly discriminatory or preferential

under Section 205 of the Federal Power Act, effective July 1, 2026, as requested by SPP.


I.       CHILLS Addresses a Genuine Reliability and Planning Problem

         The Commission recently found that “SPP has shown that unprecedented growth in large

loads in the SPP region presents significant and unique operational and planning challenges.”4


1

industry, but do not necessarily reflect the views of any particular member with respect to any issue.
2
  Sw. Power Pool, Inc., Submission of Tariff Revisions to Add Conditional High Impact Large Load Service,
Docket No. ER26-1323-000 (Feb. 2, 2026) (“CHILLS Filing”).
3
  Sw. Power Pool, Inc., 194 FERC ¶ 61,031 (2026) (“HILLs Order”).
4

 These loads, often associated with artificial intelligence, data centers, and other high-demand

facilities are arriving at a pace and scale that strain transmission planning timelines and existing

planning constructs.5 SPP explains that these large loads have unique reliability risks because

they are concentrated at a single site, are capable of rapid ramping and “load flutter,” and often

interconnect in areas already constrained by existing transmission limits. And unlike traditional

load growth, the existing tools within SPP’s toolbox are not designed to address this type of

growth.

        To solve this issue, the Commission recently accepted SPP’s HILLs framework, which

established an expedited pathway to study and interconnect large loads while preserving the

principles of open access.6 Attachment BA created additional study and operational requirements

on top of existing delivery point and transmission service processes to evaluate the unique

reliability characteristics of HILLS, including fast ramping, power-electronic behavior, and

localized system impacts.7 The framework required a dedicated HILL Delivery Point Study

(HDPS) that expanded beyond traditional steady-state analysis to include transient stability,

system strength screening, and, where warranted, Electromagnetic Transient (EMT) analysis. In

parallel, Attachment BB established the High Impact Large Load Generation Assessment

(HILLGA) process to allow localized interconnection of generation specifically identified to

support a HILL through a limited, time-bound interconnection service.8 That Load Limited

Resource Interconnection Service was constrained to serving the associated HILL, limited

geographically to nearby facilities, and did not confer ongoing transmission or interconnection

 rights, which must still be pursued through standard Tariff processes.9 HILLs created an

expedited pathway to study and interconnect large loads and supporting generation, but it did not

alter how those loads would obtain transmission services in the interim. CHILLS provides that

mechanism.

         The existing SPP Tariff requires Transmission Customers to have sufficient Designated

Resources to serve both their existing load and any new load addition.10 However, transmission

constraints often require Network Upgrades, which can take six years or more to complete. This

means “[d]uring the time between when a Transmission Customer has obtained firm

transmission service through SPP’s transmission service study process and the time that the

needed Network Upgrades are completed, loads are not able to receive the full requested Long-

Term Service or, which is often the case, no Long-Term Service at all.”11 Even where a large

load is ready to move forward, and even where generation can be brought online to support it,

SPP’s current Tariff creates a mismatch between generation and transmission. Practically

speaking, the absence of a conditional transmission mechanism means that large loads may be

forced to wait years for Network Upgrades, even where supporting generation is already in

service.12 HILLGA enables generation interconnection. CHILLS enables transmission access.

Without the latter, the former cannot function as intended.

 II.     SPP CHILLS is Just and Reasonable and Not Unduly Discriminatory or
        Preferential

        The Commission’s open-access framework is built upon transmission priority rules

designed to prevent undue discrimination and preserve open access.13 CHILLS functions within

that framework as a narrowly tailored solution that mitigates the reliability risks of large loads

through targeted operational safeguards, without interfering with open access or established

Tariff protections.

        SPP makes clear that CHILLS is a conditional, non-firm transmission service. It is

provided on an “as available” basis and is subordinate to all firm transmission rights.14

Specifically, CHILLS “will be provided by SPP using the transfer capability that is in excess of

the capability needed to serve Native Load Customers, Network Customers, other Transmission

Customers taking Long-Term Service and Short-Term Firm Point-To-Point Transmission

Service.”15 CHILLS does not allocate firm transmission rights or elevate HILL customers above

existing customers. Instead, CHILLS operates only after all firm transmission obligations are

satisfied and only so long as excess transfer capability exists.

        CHILLS also safeguards against shifting expensive Network Upgrades to existing

customers. SPP explains that “Network Upgrades will not be identified for construction to



13
   See Promoting Wholesale Competition Through Open Access Non-Discriminatory Transmission Services by
Public Utilities, Order No. 888, (April 24, 1996) at page 3-4 (“It is our statutory obligation under section 205 and
206 of the Federal Power Act (FPA) to remedy undue discrimination. To do so, we must ensure that all
[transmission] systems, including those that already provide open assess, cannot use monopoly power over
transmission to unduly discriminate against others.”); Preventing Undue Discrimination and Preference in
Transmission Service, Order No. 890, 118 FERC ¶ 61,119 at page 37 (“On systems where transmission capacity is
congested, this lack of consistency, coupled with a lack of transparency, is of heightened importance and has led to
recurring disputes over whether the transmission provider is exercising its discretion to discriminate against its
competitors. This discretion also hampers the detection of undue discrimination and, thereby, undermines the
Commission's ability to enforce the general requirement in Order No. 888 that transmission service be provided on a
not unduly discriminatory basis.”).
14
   CHILLS Filing at 13, 14-15, 28.
15
   Id. at 13.

 establish a delivery point for the sole purpose of CHILLS.”16 Instead, CHILLS “will allow

HILLs to be served by the Transmission System, at times when the Transmission System can

reliably serve the load, until the Transmission Customer for the HILL is able to obtain sufficient

Designated Resources to support Long-Term Service and/or until the needed Network Upgrades

are completed to provide the Long-Term Service.”17 CHILLS is further limited to the megawatt

(MW) amount of requested transmission service that cannot be served by the Transmission

System on a firm basis until the Network Upgrade(s) are in service.18 These provisions ensure

that CHILLS does not create de facto firm transmission rights and does not bypass upgrade

obligations. Firm deliverability remains contingent on completion of required Network

Upgrades. CHILLS simply permits conditional use of existing capacity during the interim period

before firm service becomes available.

           Importantly, CHILLS does not relieve customers of study or construction

responsibilities. While no Network Upgrades will be identified specifically to CHILLS, a

Transmission Customer and Host Transmission Owner must still construct any facilities required

pursuant to a Load Connection Study, HILL Supplemental Load Connection Study, or HILL

Load Connection Study.19 If SPP identifies a third-party impact during the study process, “the

Transmission Customer must reach an agreement with the impacted third party[.] The

Transmission Customer has until the start of the requested CHILLS or one (1) year after the

completion of the HDPS, whichever is sooner, to complete the negotiations to resolve the third-

party issues. If the third-party issues are not resolved, SPP will terminate the CHILLS.” This

prevents CHILLS from externalizing cost impacts onto neighboring systems or other

 Transmission Customers. CHILLS proceeds only where impacts are identified, studied, and

resolved.

            CHILLS is also structured as a temporary solution rather than a substitute for firm

service. Transmission Customers must submit a request for firm transmission service under

Attachment AQ or AX within one year of executing the CHILLS Agreement.20 Finally, CHILLS

“is not available for resale, redirection, reassignment, or transfer of service.”21 This restriction

prevents speculative use and ensures that CHILLS remains tied to the specific HILL for which it

was studied.

 III.   Conclusion

       SEIA supports CHILLS and the coordinated Tariff revisions. The CHILLS framework is

designed to provide a limited, conditional transmission pathway for HILLs projects by using

excess transfer capability while maintaining open access and safeguarding reliability for all

customers. The Commission should find the proposed Tariff revisions just and reasonable and

not unduly discriminatory or preferential, and accept them effective July 1, 2026.
